anatomy.intro: The ribbed body carries crosswise color bands and tiny flowering sites near the crown.

parts.function: The rounded rib is part of the succulent body.
parts.label: Fleshy rib

parts.function: Purple-brown markings cross the grey-green stem; they are coloration rather than separate leaves.
parts.label: Transverse band

parts.function: Small sites near the upper rib crests can produce cyathia, the characteristic Euphorbia flower clusters.
parts.label: Flowering eye

parts.function: The upper growing region continues the rib pattern as the body develops.
parts.label: Crown

flowers.text: The tiny cups called cyathia each contain highly reduced flowers. In wild Euphorbia obesa, separate male plants produce pollen-bearing flowers and female plants develop seed capsules; a capsule can eject its seeds when it ripens.

growth.note: In wild Euphorbia obesa, tiny leaves appear briefly and soon drop away, leaving the succulent stem as the lasting green body.

stages.text: The obesa-type body begins as a compact ball.
stages.title: Rounded youngster

stages.text: The stem enlarges while keeping its strongly grooved outline.
stages.title: Developing ribs

stages.text: The rounded stem enlarges; wild obesa becomes more cylindrical with age.
stages.title: Older form

habitat.text: Wild Euphorbia obesa grows in the Great Karoo near Graaff-Reinet in South Africa’s Eastern Cape. Its rounded, stone-like body stores water through dry periods. This is the species background of the collection’s obesa-type Dragon’s Egg selection.

lookalikes.name: Monk’s hood cactus
lookalikes.text: Both plants have rounded, ribbed bodies. Astrophytum has woolly, spine-bearing areoles; this Euphorbia has small flowering eyes along its rib crests.

mature.text: Wild Euphorbia obesa develops from a ball into a short cylinder, reaching about 20 cm high and 9 cm wide. Dragon’s Egg is grown for its compact ribbed form.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Altman Reserve.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: The cactus resemblance is an example of similar succulent shapes appearing in unrelated families. Euphorbia’s floral structure and milky latex reveal its very different botanical identity.
